H("IX. TRO / Preliminary Injunction — Opposition Plan")
P("**Relief requested (¶ 131):** (a) bar on all Greenfield direct sales to any customer in the 8-state Territory pending the action; (b) return/destruction of Confidential Sales Information under neutral supervision, with sworn certification; (c) prohibition on employing Kelsey and Ostrowski in any Territory-related capacity or any position with access to Apex information; (d) verified accounting of all Territory direct sales since Oct. 2023. Apex offers a bond in an amount set by the Court (¶ 136). Note that paragraph numbering jumps from ¶ 131 to ¶ 136 (¶¶ 132–135 missing) — confirm whether pages are missing from our copy.")
P("**Standard.** In N.C., a preliminary injunction requires a showing of likelihood of success on the merits and that the movant is likely to sustain irreparable loss unless the injunction issues, or that issuance is necessary to protect its rights during the litigation; the court also weighs the equities (A.E.P. Indus., Inc. v. McClure, 308 N.C. 393 (1983) — verify). Rule 65(b) TROs are limited in duration; Rule 65(c) requires security; Rule 65(d) requires specificity and limits who is bound. Because the hearing is on notice, expect the Court to treat it as a preliminary injunction hearing — we should be fully prepared on the merits.")
P("**Opposition themes:**")
B("**No irreparable harm / delay.** Apex knew of the direct sales and the hires by early 2024 and waited ~14 months to sue; ¶ 139’s claim of prompt action is contradicted by its own dates. Its claimed injuries are historic, already quantified to the dollar ($4.26M in sales; $766,800; $1,491,000; $6.2M NPV), and compensable in money. The customers have already moved (¶ 55); an injunction cannot restore them.")
B("**Likelihood of success is weakest exactly where the most intrusive relief is sought.** Even if Apex is likely to win on renewal, that supports at most narrowly tailored relief through Feb. 28, 2026 — not mandatory return/destruction, an accounting, or employment restrictions, all of which depend on the trade-secret theory that Exhibit E’s chronology undermines.")
B("**Overbreadth.** Request (a) would bar sales to every customer in eight states, including N.C., where Greenfield is headquartered, and including customers Apex never served; it would harm third-party customers who rely on Greenfield for spare parts, service and urgent replacements (public interest). Request (d) is discovery dressed as an injunction. Request (b) presupposes possession of materials Apex has not shown exist.")
B("**Non-parties and statutory bars.** Request (c) would effectively enjoin non-parties’ employment on the basis of contracts that Greenfield is not party to, that are not sued upon, and whose enforceability is contested; the DTSA forbids injunctions preventing employment and requires evidence of threatened misappropriation (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)); Georgia rejects inevitable disclosure as an independent basis.")
B("**Mandatory relief alters the status quo.** The last peaceable status quo since March 2024 is that Greenfield sells directly; requests (b) and (d) are mandatory and require a heightened showing.")
B("**Evidentiary weakness.** The verification is on “knowledge, information, and belief,” and the key trade-secret facts are pleaded on information and belief — insufficient to support emergency relief.")
B("**Bond.** If any relief issues, request substantial security under Rule 65(c) reflecting Greenfield’s projected lost Territory sales and customer-relationship harm through Feb. 28, 2026 (client to supply run-rate data). P("**Defensive interim measures (strongly recommended before May 9):** (i) written instructions that Kelsey and Ostrowski not use or disclose any Apex information; (ii) sworn certifications from each that they retained no Apex documents, after forensic confirmation; (iii) temporary screening of both from the four accounts and from pricing for those accounts; (iv) consideration of an offered, without-prejudice stipulated order embodying (i)–(iii) plus document preservation, in exchange for withdrawal of requests (a), (c) and (d). A business decision is also needed on whether Greenfield would offer, without prejudice, to route Territory sales through Apex (or to pay a margin into escrow) through Feb. 28, 2026; that would substantially undercut irreparable harm and cap Count I damages, but it has commercial costs the client must weigh.")

23:**Bottom line.** Apex pleads four counts and a headline demand of \$22,341,800 (plus punitive and exemplary damages, fees, and interest). The headline number is substantially inflated: it stacks overlapping measures of the same loss, pleads unjust enrichment in the alternative but adds it to the total anyway, and rests its trade-secret theory on a timeline that Apex's own exhibits contradict. Greenfield nonetheless faces genuine liability risk on the core contract claim. Our preliminary, non-duplicative assessment of realistic compensatory exposure is roughly **\$1.5 million to \$7 million**, with a most-likely band of approximately **\$3--6 million plus fee-shifting**, and a serious adverse-case exposure in the **\$11--16 million** range (before fees and interest) if a jury accepts Apex's renewal theory, its lost-profit model, and a willful trade-secret finding (see Part VIII).
25:**Greenfield's most critical vulnerabilities (candidly):**
27:- **The non-renewal notices very likely failed.** Section 4.2 requires a notice "delivered by the Chief Executive Officer or General Counsel" at least 180 days before expiration and expressly declares a non-compliant notice "void and of no force or effect," naming "the signatory and timing requirements." The July 15, 2023 notice was signed by the VP of Sales; the September 12, 2023 CEO notice gave only 169 days. Our count confirms Ms. Yuen's: 169 days (the 180-day cut-off was in fact September 1, 2023, so the letter was 11 days late). The express voidness clause largely forecloses substantial-compliance arguments, and Greenfield never answered Apex's August 3, 2023 objection letter, which flagged the defect four weeks before the deadline. The September 12 letter also states that it "supersedes and replaces" the July 15 notice, which undercuts any ratification theory.
29:- **The direct sales occurred during the undisputed Initial Term.** Every Exhibit E invoice is dated between November 15, 2023 and February 5, 2024 --- before the Initial Term expired on February 28, 2024. Liability for those \$4.26 million in sales therefore does not depend on the renewal dispute at all; if the (omitted) exclusivity grant in Articles I--III bars manufacturer direct sales, that breach is close to strict liability. The client email's account that Mr. Hargrove was "eager to begin Greenfield's direct sales efforts in the Southeast" will be discoverable as a fact and is unhelpful on intent.
31:- **The Year 2 shortfall is a weak defense.** Greenfield never sent a Section 5.3 cure notice, never invoked Section 12.1(b), and accepted three more years of above-minimum performance. Waiver/estoppel and course-of-dealing arguments favor Apex, and an affirmative counterclaim on the 2020--21 shortfall faces a serious limitations problem in a North Carolina forum (Part VII.B).
33:- **Hiring diligence on Kelsey and Ostrowski is uncertain.** Ms. Yuen is not certain anyone reviewed their Apex agreements before offers were extended. Knowledge is an element of the interference theory and of willfulness under the trade secret statutes.
35:**Greenfield's strongest defensive themes:**
37:- **Apex's trade-secret causation story collapses on its own exhibits.** Apex alleges (¶ 111) that the direct sales "commenced within weeks of" the February 2024 hires and that Greenfield used the employees' pricing data to undercut Apex (¶¶ 54, 104, 112). But the Magnolia (Nov. 15, 2023), Tidewater (Dec. 8, 2023 and Jan. 22, 2024) and Clearwater (Jan. 18, 2024) invoices --- \$2.71 million of the \$4.26 million --- predate the hires. Only the Southeastern Bottling invoice (Feb. 5, 2024) is even contemporaneous. Apex also pleads that Greenfield's own records already showed every prior sale to these customers (¶¶ 53, 88), which undermines secrecy of customer identity as against Greenfield.

Our preliminary, non-duplicative assessment of realistic compensatory exposure is roughly **\$1.5 million to \$7 million**, with a most-likely band of approximately **\$3--6 million plus fee-shifting**, and a serious adverse-case exposure in the **\$11--16 million** range (before fees and interest) if a jury accepts Apex's renewal theory, its lost-profit model, and a willful trade-secret finding (see Part VIII).

**Greenfield's most critical vulnerabilities (candidly):**

- **The non-renewal notices very likely failed.** Section 4.2 requires a notice "delivered by the Chief Executive Officer or General Counsel" at least 180 days before expiration and expressly declares a non-compliant notice "void and of no force or effect," naming "the signatory and timing requirements." The July 15, 2023 notice was signed by the VP of Sales; the September 12, 2023 CEO notice gave only 169 days. Our count confirms Ms. Yuen's: 169 days (the 180-day cut-off was in fact September 1, 2023, so the letter was 11 days late). The express voidness clause largely forecloses substantial-compliance arguments, and Greenfield never answered Apex's August 3, 2023 objection letter, which flagged the defect four weeks before the deadline. The September 12 letter also states that it "supersedes and replaces" the July 15 notice, which undercuts any ratification theory.

- **The direct sales occurred during the undisputed Initial Term.** Every Exhibit E invoice is dated between November 15, 2023 and February 5, 2024 --- before the Initial Term expired on February 28, 2024. Liability for those \$4.26 million in sales therefore does not depend on the renewal dispute at all; if the (omitted) exclusivity grant in Articles I--III bars manufacturer direct sales, that breach is close to strict liability. The client email's account that Mr. Hargrove was "eager to begin Greenfield's direct sales efforts in the Southeast" will be discoverable as a fact and is unhelpful on intent.

- **The Year 2 shortfall is a weak defense.** Greenfield never sent a Section 5.3 cure notice, never invoked Section 12.1(b), and accepted three more years of above-minimum performance. Waiver/estoppel and course-of-dealing arguments favor Apex, and an affirmative counterclaim on the 2020--21 shortfall faces a serious limitations problem in a North Carolina forum (Part VII.B).

- **Hiring diligence on Kelsey and Ostrowski is uncertain.** Ms. Yuen is not certain anyone reviewed their Apex agreements before offers were extended. Knowledge is an element of the interference theory and of willfulness under the trade secret statutes.

**Greenfield's strongest defensive themes:**

- **Apex's trade-secret causation story collapses on its own exhibits.** Apex alleges (¶ 111) that the direct sales "commenced within weeks of" the February 2024 hires and that Greenfield used the employees' pricing data to undercut Apex (¶¶ 54, 104, 112). But the Magnolia (Nov. 15, 2023), Tidewater (Dec. 8, 2023 and Jan. 22, 2024) and Clearwater (Jan. 18, 2024) invoices --- \$2.71 million of the \$4.26 million --- predate the hires. Only the Southeastern Bottling invoice (Feb. 5, 2024) is even contemporaneous. Apex also pleads that Greenfield's own records already showed every prior sale to these customers (¶¶ 53, 88), which undermines secrecy of customer identity as against Greenfield.

- **Delay defeats emergency relief.** Apex knew of the direct sales and the hires by early 2024, yet filed roughly 14 months after the last identified invoice (442 days after Feb. 5, 2024). The harm Apex describes (lost customers) has already occurred and is quantified to the dollar in the Complaint, which supports an adequate remedy at law.
